newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco plans reform to speed up privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Morocco plans reform to speed up privatisation.

text.p: Morocco plans to draw up a fresh list of companies slated for privatisation and change the way the programme operates to speed up the sale of state holdings and give more flexibility on pricing.
Privatisation Minister Abderrahman Saadi, in remarks published on Thursday, said: "There are two reform projects. The first is on procedures. The one now in place is too slow.

"Moreover, we have noticed that our way of determining the price is too administrative. While each of us can set a value on something, only the market can determine the price which is only defined if the transaction goes ahead."
Moroccan law now demands the Evaluation Organisation sets the price for shares sold in state companies, and there has been criticism that the programme is too slow and cumbersome.
"We are proposing (to parliament) that the Evaluation Organisation sets an indication price, a reference price, and that the market will decide," the minister said.
"In addition, it is proposed that the investment programme of a potential purchaser and his projects for employment, as well as his experience in the sector, are included in the selection criteria."
These criteria "may not count for more than 15 percent of the price proposed by the candidate making the best offer," he added.
Morocco started its privatisation programme in November 1993 and has so far sold stakes in 46 companies. A total of 114 are on the list for sale of state holdings by the end of 1998.
Saadi, without giving detail, said: "The government has given me a mandate to prepare, with other departments...a new list of enterprises to privatise or restructure."
But he added that opening up telecommunications to the private sector "appears very opportune with the technological evoluation and alliances being made across the world in this area."
One of Morocco's biggest privatisation projects is for the SAMIR company, the country's main oil plant in which the government expects to sell a stake of up to 51 percent to foreign oil investors.

Saadi told Le Matin du Sahara et du Maghreb newspaper that a study was now being carried out on the navigation COMANAV while privatisation of Royal Air Maroc (RAM), the state airline was a "theoretical possibility."

RAM operates 27 aircrafts, mainly Boeings, and made a net profit of 74 million dirhams ($8.5 million) in the first eight months of 1996, carrying 1.8 million passengers -- 8.3 percent more than the same period the previous year.
